## Solution

We determine all real $x$ for which
$$S = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2+n}\,\tan^2\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\right) n^x$$
converges.

**General term.** Write
$$a_n = \frac{n^x}{n(n+1)}\tan^2\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\right).$$

**Asymptotics of the tangent factor.** Since $\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\to 0$ and $\tan t \sim t$ as $t\to 0$,
$$\tan^2\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\right) \sim \frac{1}{n}.$$

**Limit comparison.** Compare $a_n$ with $n^{x-3}$:
$$\frac{a_n}{n^{x-3}} = \frac{n^3}{n(n+1)}\tan^2\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\right) = \frac{n^2}{n+1}\tan^2\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\right).$$

Set $t = 1/\sqrt n$ (so $t\to 0^+$ as $n\to\infty$); then $n = 1/t^2$ and
$$\frac{n^2}{n+1} = \frac{1/t^4}{1/t^2+1} = \frac{1}{t^2(1+t^2)}.$$
Hence
$$\frac{a_n}{n^{x-3}} = \frac{\tan^2 t}{t^2(1+t^2)} = \left(\frac{\tan t}{t}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{1+t^2} \;\xrightarrow{t\to 0}\; 1\cdot 1 = 1.$$

So
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{n^{x-3}} = 1 > 0.$$

**Applying the limit comparison test.** Since the limit is a positive finite constant, $\sum a_n$ converges if and only if $\sum n^{x-3}$ converges. The $p$-series $\sum n^{x-3}$ converges exactly when its exponent satisfies $x-3 < -1$, i.e.
$$x < 2.$$

**Boundary check.** At $x=2$, $a_n \sim n^{-1}$, so the series diverges (harmonic). For $x>2$ it diverges a fortiori. For $x<2$ the comparison gives convergence.

## Conclusion

The series converges precisely for
$$\boxed{x < 2}, \qquad \text{i.e. } x\in(-\infty,\,2).$$
